content.title: About
content.content: Chicken wing, fried, coated are pieces of chicken meat covered with a crispy breading and deep‑fried until golden. They are a popular fast‑food item and restaurant snack, served as an appetizer or part of a main dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Wings are often served with a variety of sauces: barbecue, hot, honey‑mustard.
The tradition of deep‑fried wings in the US began in the 1960s, becoming a staple of "barbecue" and "spicy" menus.
Breading can include flour, corn starch, spices, and breadcrumbs, giving different flavors and textures.
Chicken wings are a favorite bar food, especially during sports broadcasts.
In some countries, such as Japan, fried wings are served as "tenkatsu" with soy‑based sauces.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Chicken provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Wings contain niacin, vitamin B6 and B12, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: They provide iron, zinc and phosphorus, important for blood formation and bone health.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: Fried wings deliver quick calories, useful for people with high energy needs.

items.title: Collagen content
items.content: The skin and connective tissue are rich in collagen, beneficial for skin and joint health.

items.title: High fat and calorie content
items.content: Deep‑frying adds saturated fats and calories, which can contribute to weight gain if eaten frequently.

items.title: Trans fats
items.content: Repeated use of oil can create trans fats, which are harmful to cardiovascular health.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: Some individuals may have allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: Salt and additives
items.content: Breading often contains salt and flavor enhancers, which may be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Acrylamide formation
items.content: Improper frying temperatures can produce acrylamide, a potential carcinogen.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve wings hot, typically with dipping sauces. They can be eaten as a snack, added to salads, rice or noodle dishes, or used in "wing‑in‑batter" recipes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked wings in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze them in a freezer‑safe bag for up to 2 months. Reheat thoroughly to an internal temperature of 75 °C before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Animal-shaped cookie with frosting is a sweet treat molded into various animal figures and coated with a smooth sugar or buttercream frosting. The dough is typically made from wheat flour, butter, sugar, and eggs, and after baking the pieces are decorated with bright frosting, often tinted with food coloring.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The animal shapes make the cookies especially popular with children and at themed parties.
Frosting can be either sugar-based or butter-based, allowing a range of flavors and textures.
These cookies are traditionally prepared for the holiday season in many European and North American cultures.
Special metal or plastic cutters are used to achieve detailed animal silhouettes.
They are often sold in assortments where each piece represents a different animal.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Provides carbohydrates that quickly replenish energy stores.

items.title: B‑vitamin content
items.content: Whole‑grain versions of the dough supply modest amounts of B1, B2, and niacin.

items.title: Calcium from frosting
items.content: If the frosting contains milk powder, it can contribute a small amount of calcium.

items.title: Gluten and dairy allergy
items.content: Traditional recipes contain wheat flour and dairy, which may trigger reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: The frosting adds significant sugar, so consumption should be moderate, especially for children.

items.title: Choking hazard for young children
items.content: Small or hard animal figures can pose a choking risk for toddlers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the cookies as a standalone snack, use them to decorate cakes, cupcakes, or ice cream, or serve them as themed treats at children’s parties.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, store in the refrigerator to prevent the frosting from softening. Avoid exposure to direct sunlight.

content.title: About
content.content: Pastry, egg and cheese filled is a baked good made from flaky pastry dough and a rich mixture of eggs, cheese, and sometimes herbs. It features a crisp outer layer and a creamy, savory filling, making it a popular snack in cafés and street food stalls.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The tradition of stuffing pastries with egg and cheese dates back to Mediterranean culinary practices.
Flaky pastry for these items is often hand‑laminated, rolled and folded multiple times to create many layers.
Some regional recipes add spices such as paprika or black pepper to the filling for extra flavor.
These pastries are usually served hot, straight from the oven, so the filling stays warm and slightly runny.
They are conveniently packaged in paper boxes, which makes them a favorite for food‑delivery services.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Eggs and cheese provide complete protein essential for tissue repair and maintenance.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Cheese contributes calcium that supports bone and dental health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs supply vitamin B12 and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains vitamin D
items.content: Certain cheeses contain vitamin D, which aids calcium absorption.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: The combination of carbohydrates from the pastry and fats from the cheese provides quick energy.

items.title: Egg or dairy allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to eggs or milk proteins may experience reactions.

items.title: High fat and calorie content
items.content: Flaky pastry and cheese make the product calorie‑dense; portion control is advised for weight management.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Cheese is often salty, so people with hypertension should limit intake.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Improper storage can allow bacterial growth, especially Salmonella, in the egg filling.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Best enjoyed hot, reheated in an oven or microwave. It can be eaten as a standalone snack or paired with a salad, yogurt dip, or tomato sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated in an airtight container for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze in a freezer‑safe bag for up to 2 months; reheat to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C before consumption.

pizza-with-meat-other-than-pepperoni-fro.title: Pizza with meat other than pepperoni

content.title: About
content.content: Pizza with meat other than pepperoni is an Italian‑style dish that uses toppings such as ham, salami, sausage, bacon or chicken breast instead of pepperoni. The crust can be thin or medium, topped with tomato sauce and mozzarella cheese.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Meat‑topped pizzas are common in fast‑food chains and casual restaurants for a quick protein boost.
Mixing different meats creates a variety of flavors and aromas in each pizza.
The classic Italian “Quattro Formaggi” is sometimes enhanced with meat, but traditionally without pepperoni.
In the United States, chicken‑BBQ and bacon pizzas are popular as milder alternatives to pepperoni.
Dough enriched with olive oil yields a crispier crust.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Meat toppings provide high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Red meats like ham or salami supply heme iron, which supports oxygen transport.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat contributes vitamins B12, B6 and niacin, important for metabolism.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Mozzarella adds calcium that helps maintain strong bones.

items.title: Antioxidants from tomato sauce
items.content: Tomatoes are rich in lycopene, a powerful antioxidant.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Processed meats such as sausage and ham often contain a lot of salt, which can be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Bacon and some sausages are high in saturated fat, which should be limited in heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Mozzarella may trigger reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk allergy.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Meat‑topped pizza is usually calorie‑rich; portion control is advisable, especially on weight‑loss plans.

items.title: Proper cooking
items.content: Undercooked meat can harbor pathogens; ensure all toppings are fully cooked.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice the pizza into wedges and serve hot. Fresh toppings such as tomatoes, arugula, or a drizzle of olive oil or BBQ sauce can be added after baking for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat in an oven or grill to restore crust crispness.

potato-roasted-from-fresh-peel-not-eaten.title: Potato, roasted, from fresh, peel not eaten, fat added, fat type not specified (4170)

content.title: About
content.content: Roasted potatoes are made from fresh tubers that are peeled and cooked in oil. The process retains most of the starch while the added fat increases calories and gives a rich flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Potatoes are one of the most widely consumed vegetables worldwide.
Roasting creates a golden crust where aromatic compounds such as aldehydes and pyrazines develop.
There are many roasting methods: deep‑fat frying, shallow pan‑frying, or oven‑roasting with a small amount of oil.
French fries, a popular form of roasted potato, originated in Belgium in the late 19th century.
The fat content of roasted potatoes depends on the type and amount of oil used.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Potatoes are rich in carbohydrates that quickly convert to glucose, providing readily available energy.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: They contain vitamin B6, which supports protein metabolism and neurotransmitter synthesis.

items.title: Potassium
items.content: Potassium helps maintain fluid balance and normal blood pressure.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Even without the skin, the flesh provides a modest amount of fiber that aids digestion.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Potatoes contain carotenoids and phenolic compounds that may protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Added fat markedly raises the calorie count, so portion control is important.

items.title: Trans fats and oxidized oil
items.content: Re‑using oil can generate trans fats and harmful oxidation products.

items.title: Acrylamide formation
items.content: High‑temperature cooking can produce acrylamide, a potential carcinogen.

items.title: Oil allergy
items.content: People allergic to certain vegetable oils may experience reactions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Roasted potatoes are served as a side dish, in wedges, slices, or sticks. They can be seasoned with salt, herbs, spices, or paired with sauces such as ketchup, mayo, or sour cream.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked roasted potatoes in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 2–3 days. Reheat in an oven or skillet to restore crispness.

potato-roasted-from-fresh-peel-not-eaten.title: Potato, roasted, from fresh, peel not eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Roasted potato from fresh product is made of peeled potato pieces fried until golden. The peel is not consumed. Potatoes are rich in carbohydrates, vitamin C, potassium and a small amount of protein.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Potatoes were introduced to Europe from South America in the 16th century.
Frying creates a characteristic aroma through the Maillard reaction.
There are over 4,000 potato varieties, but high‑starch types are preferred for roasting.
Potato chips first appeared in the United States in 1853.
Potato skins contain more fiber and nutrients than the flesh.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports heart function.

items.title: Vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C acts as an antioxidant and supports the immune system.

items.title: Energy-providing carbs
items.content: Carbohydrates in potatoes quickly supply the body with energy.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids normal digestive function.

items.title: Low sodium content
items.content: When not salted, roasted potatoes contain little sodium.

items.title: High fat content from frying
items.content: Frying increases calories and saturated fat levels.

items.title: Acrylamide formation
items.content: High temperatures can produce acrylamide, a potential carcinogen.

items.title: Potato allergy
items.content: Rarely, some individuals may experience an allergic reaction.

items.title: Possible food poisoning
items.content: Raw or undercooked pieces may contain solanine, a toxin destroyed by proper cooking.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Roasted potatoes are served as a side dish, in slices, wedges or cubes. They can be seasoned with herbs, spices or a light pinch of salt. The peel is usually removed before frying, though it can be used after thorough cleaning.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh potatoes in a cool, dark place, avoiding moisture. Roasted potatoes should be kept in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days.

spaghetti-sauce-with-poultry-and-added-v.title: Spaghetti sauce with poultry and added vegetables

content.title: About
content.content: Spaghetti sauce with poultry and added vegetables is a ready‑to‑eat tomato‑based sauce enriched with pieces of chicken breast and a blend of carrots, celery, onion and sweet pepper. It is designed for quick preparation of a complete meal, combining aromatic herbs, spices and the natural sweetness of vegetables.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The sauce contains real chicken meat, not just flavor enhancers.
Vegetables are added fresh during processing, preserving texture and nutrients.
The tomato base provides a high level of lycopene, a powerful antioxidant.
The product undergoes heat treatment, making it safe for long‑term storage without preservatives.
The combination of protein and vegetables creates a balanced energy source for active people.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Chicken pieces supply high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Both the poultry and vegetables provide vitamin B6 and niacin, supporting metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Lycopene and antioxidants
items.content: Tomatoes are abundant in lycopene, which helps protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: The vegetable mix adds soluble and insoluble fiber, promoting healthy digestion.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: The recipe uses minimal added oils, making it suitable for diets limiting saturated fat.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to poultry may experience reactions when consuming the sauce.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Like many ready sauces, it can contain a relatively high amount of salt; people monitoring sodium intake should watch portion size.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Flavorings or thickeners may contain gluten; check the label if you have celiac disease.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Some batches may include preservatives for shelf life; those sensitive should choose preservative‑free versions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the sauce in a saucepan or microwave, add cooked spaghetti and stir. You can finish with fresh herbs, grated Parmesan, or a drizzle of olive oil. The sauce also works as a base for casseroles, risotto, or vegetable stews.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened package in a cool, dry place at up to 25 °C. After opening, keep it refrigerated and consume within 5 days. Discard if you notice off‑odors or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Frozen strawberries are ripe berries harvested at peak season, quickly frozen at low temperatures to preserve flavor, aroma, and nutrients. The berries are usually trimmed of stems and leaves before being packed in airtight bags.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Strawberries are one of the most popular berries worldwide, cultivated in over 30 countries.
Freezing occurs within minutes of harvest, retaining up to 90 % of vitamin C.
Frozen strawberries are commonly used in smoothies, desserts, and sauces.
Antioxidant levels, such as anthocyanins, remain high after freezing.
In the United States, more than 1.5 million tons of frozen strawberries are consumed each year.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Anthocyanins and flavonoids help combat free radicals and reduce inflammation.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: A 100 g serving provides about 30 kcal, making it an excellent choice for weight management.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and contributes to satiety.

items.title: Supports heart health
items.content: Phytonutrients can help lower blood pressure and cholesterol levels.

items.title: Berry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to strawberries.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Strawberries contain natural sugars; people with diabetes should monitor portion sizes.

items.title: Freezing quality
items.content: Improper storage can cause ice crystal formation and texture loss.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Frozen strawberries can be added to smoothies, yogurts, oatmeal, baked goods, sauces, and ice cream. They can be slightly thawed in the refrigerator or used directly in hot dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen strawberries in their original airtight bag at –18 °C or lower. After opening, transfer to a sealed container to prevent moisture and odor absorption. Use within 12 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Shrimp sushi is a traditional Japanese dish consisting of vinegared rice topped with fresh shrimp, usually served with soy sauce, wasabi, and pickled ginger. The shrimp adds a delicate sea flavor and an extra source of protein.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sushi originated in Southeast Asia as a method of preserving fish in rice.
Shrimp is often used in nigiri – a slice of seafood placed on a small mound of rice.
Japan boasts over 200 types of sushi, but shrimp sushi remains one of the most popular among tourists.
Traditionally shrimp are served raw, but in some regions they are lightly boiled or seared.
Sushi is commonly eaten with chopsticks, though using hands is also acceptable in Japan.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Shrimp provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many meat dishes, shrimp sushi is low in fat, making it suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Source of omega‑3
items.content: Shrimp contains beneficial omega‑3 fatty acids that support heart and vascular health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Sushi supplies vitamins B12 and B6, important for nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Shrimp is a good source of selenium, zinc, and iodine, which aid thyroid function and immunity.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience severe allergic reactions to shrimp.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Raw shrimp can harbor bacteria and parasites; only fresh, high‑quality shrimp should be used.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce commonly served with sushi is high in salt, which can be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Digestive issues
items.content: Large amounts of rice may cause discomfort for those with sensitive stomachs.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pick up a piece with chopsticks or your hand, dip lightly in soy sauce, add a touch of wasabi, and eat in one bite. Pickled ginger is served to cleanse the palate between different sushi types.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store prepared sushi in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C and consume within 24 hours. The rice can lose its texture quickly, so it is best enjoyed soon after preparation.
